The eighteen-eighty-nine Paris Exposition Universelle was held in celebration of the centennial of the French Revolution. The fair introduced the world to the Eiffel Tower, designed by engineer Gustave Eiffel. This engineering marvel became the fair's defining symbol and one of history's most recognisable structures, standing at three hundred twenty-four meters tall, making it the world's tallest building at the time. Interestingly, Gustave Eiffel's bold design faced fierce criticism from many Parisian artists before the fair's opening. Despite the initial hostility toward his vision, the tower became beloved and has remained a permanent fixture ever since. Beyond the tower, the fair displayed significant innovations in electricity, lighting, and transportation that showcased France's technological prowess during the Belle Époque period. The exposition also introduced the Palais des Machines, a massive iron and glass hall that demonstrated advanced structural engineering and pushed the boundaries of what was considered architecturally possible. Nearly thirty-two million visitors came from across Europe and beyond to experience the fair, making it a resounding success. The exposition celebrated a hundred years of French republican ideals and industrial progress. The fair established a new template for ambitious world's fairs globally, with the Eiffel Tower establishing the convention that major expositions should feature a monumental centrepiece icon.
